source_title: Walter Koenig, Chekov on Original ‘Star Trek,’ Dies at 90
source_excerpt:
Walter Koenig, Chekov on Original ‘Star Trek,’ Dies at 90 6 days ago

Walter Koenig , who memorably played Chekov in the original “ Star Trek ” series and seven “Star Trek” feature films, died Sunday in Los Angeles, Variety has confirmed. He was 90.
His reps said in a statement, “Today we mourn the passing of Walter Koenig, whose talent, warmth, and unforgettable performances left a lasting mark on generations of fans around the world. “Best known for his iconic role as Pavel Chekov in ‘Star Trek: The Original Series,’ Walter helped inspire audiences with his optimism, humor, and adventurous spirit. Beyond ‘Star Trek,’ his long and distinguished career showcased his versatility as an actor and his genuine love for his craft. His remarkable talent continued to shine in his later years, most recently with his performance in the short film ‘Mr. Fleischmann,’ for which he received the Platinum Award for Best Actor at the 2026 Independent Shorts Awards — a fitting recognition of a lifetime devoted to his craft.
“Walter’s legacy extends far beyond the screen. Through countless convention appearances and interactions with fans, he shared his kindness, wit, and appreciation with everyone fortunate enough to meet him. He understood what Star Trek meant to people and embraced the community that grew around it.
“On behalf of all of us, we extend our deepest condolences to Walter’s family, friends, colleagues, and the millions of fans whose lives he touched over the decades.
“Thank you, Walter, for the memories, the inspiration, and for boldly going where few have gone before.”
Koenig’s Chekov, an arrogant young navigation officer in the original series, was introduced to the series to appeal to teenage viewers — his hairstyle recalled that of the Monkees’ Davy Jones.
The Russian-born Chekov was also used to poke fun at the Soviet way of falsely taking credit for every important human invention.
Koenig played Chekov in the 2015 TV movie “Star Trek: Renegades,” set at a time in which the character has been elevated to admiral. The film, aimed as a backdoor pilot for a new “Star Trek” television series, was funded through crowdsourcing.
The Chekov character was not included in “Star Trek: The Animated Series” in the early ’70s because of the show’s limited budget, but Koenig penned an episode of the series entitled “The Infinite Vulcan.”
Koenig’s Chekov was central to the plot of 1982’s “Star Trek II: The Wrath of Khan” and consequently the actor enjoyed considerable screen time in the film, generally considered the best of the “Star Trek” movies.
Koenig was also associated with another sci-fi franchise, J. Michael Straczynski’s “ Babylon 5 ,” in which he played the evil Psi Cop Alfred Bester (named by the show’s creators after the science fiction writer). He appeared in 12 episodes of that show from 1994-98.
Walter Marvin Koenig was born in Chicago. The family of Russian Jewish heritage was originally named Koenigsberg, and he attended Fieldston High School in Fieldston, N.Y., where he did some stage work, before starting at Grinnell College in Iowa, where he was initially pre-med; he transferred to and graduated from UCLA with a degree in psychology. After a professor urged him to pursue a career in acting, he began studying at the Neighborhood Playhouse in New York; there his classmates included Christopher Lloyd, with whom he would be reunited on “Star Trek III: The Search for Spock,” in which Lloyd played the villainous Klingon Commander Kruge, as well as James Caan and Dabney Coleman.
Koenig made his small-screen debut with an uncredited role in an episode of “Combat!” in 1962, followed by guest-starring roles on “The Untouchables,” “General Hospital,” “The Alfred Hitchcock Hour,” “Ben Casey,” “Gidget” and “I Spy.” After the original “Star Trek” series went off the air in 1969, he worked occasionally in TV, guesting on “The Virginian,” “Ironside” and “Columbo” (in an episode that had William Shatner as the special guest star). He played a deputy sheriff in an unremarkable low-budget film called “Nightmare Honeymoon,” starring Dack Rambo.
During the 1980s, when he was busy with the “Star Trek” movies, he appeared as Pompey in a 1984 TV adaptation of “Antony & Cleopatra” that also featured Nichelle Nichols and future “Star Trek: Enterprise” actor James Avery.
The actor appeared in a string of low-budget science fiction movies over the years, including “Moontrap,” in which he starred, and “Deadly Weapon,” both in 1989; as well as Cynthia Rothrock martial arts vehicle “Sworn to Justice” in 1996 and independent horror film “Mad Cowgirl” in 2006.
A one-character film that Koenig wrote and performed, “You’re Never Alone When You’re a Schizophrenic,” was screened at the 1996 New York Film Festival.
He voiced Chekov in a variety of “Star Trek” video games, including 1998’s “Starfleet Academy: Chekov’s Lost Missions.”
The actor guested on an episode of the CBS sitcom “Almost Perfect” titled “Where No Woman Has Gone Before” in 1997 and voiced himself on a 2002 episode of “Futurama” titled “Where No Fan Has Gone Before,” which also featured the voices of William Shatner and Leonard Nimoy, among other “Star Trek” regulars. He also guested on “Diagnosis Murder” (in an episode that featured several other “Star Trek” actors) and “Son of the Beach.”
He penned the 2008 sci-fi legal thriller “InAlienable,” in which he also appeared (the tagline was “From the mind of Walter Koenig”).
Koenig also had a stage career that spanned three decades.
In the early 1990s he toured with Mark Lenard (who played Spock’s father Sarek on “Star Trek”) in “The Boys in Autumn,” in which Koenig played a middle-aged Tom Sawyer reunited after decades apart with Lenard’s Huckleberry Finn.
Koenig also directed theater, including “Hotel Parsadiso” for Company of Angels, “Becket” for Theatre 40, “America Hurrah!” at Oxford Theater, “Twelve Angry Men” at the Rita Hayworth Theatre, “Matrix” at the Gascon Theatre Institute and “Three by Ten” at Actors Alley in Los Angeles.
Koenig taught acting classes at UCLA, at Actors Alley and elsewhere.
His satiric fantasy novel “Buck Alice and the Actor-Robot” was re-released in 2006; he created the comic book “Raver” published by Malibu Comics. In 2013 Bluewater Comics published the graphic novel “Walter Koenig’s Things to Come.”
Koenig penned the memoirs “Chekov’s Enterprise: A Personal Journal of the Making of Star Trek — The Motion Picture,” published in 1980, and “Warped Factors — A Neurotic’s Guide to the Universe,” published in 1998.
Anton Yelchin portrayed a much younger Chekov in the rebooted “Star Trek” films.
Back in the days of the original “Star Trek” series there was a period of tension between Koenig and George Takei, who played Sulu, but the two came to be close friends, and in September 2008, Koenig served as best man at Takei’s wedding to Brad Altman.
Koenig a daughter, actress-writer Danielle Koenig. A son, actor and editor Andrew Koenig, died in 2010.
